7174.title: Normal Equation
7174.heading: Normal Equation
7174.content:
For a least squares problem $Ax\approx b$, the normal equation is $A^TA\hat x=A^Tb$. It expresses that the residual $b-A\hat x$ is orthogonal to every column of $A$.

If the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the equation has the unique solution $(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb$. Forming $A^TA$ can worsen conditioning, so [[QR Decomposition]] or [[Singular Value Decomposition]] may be more stable.

For the source's linear-model notation, the equation is $X^T X\hat\beta=X^T Y$. It explains the mathematics behind R's `lm` result while also showing why production implementations do not need to form the displayed inverse directly.

7177.title: Normal Stress
7177.heading: Normal Stress
7177.content:
Normal stress is internal axial force divided by the cross-sectional area over which it acts. Tensile stress is positive when it tends to lengthen a member, while compressive stress is negative when it tends to shorten it.

Because stress scales force by member size, it permits comparison among rods with different areas. In a bar element, stress is recovered from nodal displacement through the material modulus and strain-displacement relation.

7180.title: Nonverbal Communication
7180.heading: Nonverbal Communication
7180.content:
Nonverbal communication conveys interactional meaning through gaze, facial expression, gesture, posture, movement, timing, and spatial orientation. In an embodied assistant, these signals can show attention, turn readiness, emphasis, or uncertainty.

Signals must agree with speech and dialog state. A [[Social Robot]] that speaks to one person while looking at another can create confusion even when every word is correct.

7183.title: Nonsingular Matrix
7183.heading: Nonsingular Matrix
7183.content:
A nonsingular matrix is a [[Square Matrix]] with nonzero [[Determinant]]. It has a unique [[Matrix Inverse]], full rank, and exactly one solution to $Ax=b$ for every compatible right-hand side.

Nonsingularity also means the matrix can be reduced to the [[Identity Matrix]] and expressed as a product of [[Elementary Matrix|elementary matrices]].

7189.title: Nonrepudiation
7189.heading: Nonrepudiation
7189.content:
Nonrepudiation supplies evidence that the source of information or an online action can be validated later. It reduces the ability of a sender to deny sending a message or of a participant to deny completing a recorded transaction.

The source describes it as a combination of authentication and integrity. [[Digital Signature|Digital signatures]] and [[Message Authentication Code|message authentication codes]] can bind message evidence to protected keys, while delivery and transaction records preserve the relevant context.

7192.title: Nonlinear Programming
7192.heading: Nonlinear Programming
7192.content:
Nonlinear programming optimizes an objective when the objective or at least one constraint is nonlinear. Nonlinearity may come from powers, products of variables, trigonometric functions, exponentials, or logarithms.

Unlike [[Linear Programming]], an optimum need not occur at an extreme point. Solution methods use derivatives, nonlinear equations, local searches, and constraint conditions, so convexity strongly affects whether a local result is globally optimal.

The nonnegativity constraint produces additive representations and often makes components easier to interpret than signed factors. Cluster assignments can be taken from dominant component weights or coupled directly to a partitioning objective.

7198.title: Nonlinearity
7198.heading: Nonlinearity
7198.content:
Nonlinearity occurs when a change in input does not produce a proportional change in output. Interacting feedback loops can create thresholds, oscillations, acceleration, or collapse that a linear projection would miss.

Nonlinear behavior is central to many [[Complex System|complex systems]] and [[Progression Curve|progression curves]]. It can expand a game's decision space, but it also makes prediction and balancing more difficult.

A nonhomogeneous linear system has the form $Ax=b$ with a nonzero right-hand side. Unlike a [[Homogeneous Linear System]], it may be consistent or inconsistent.

When it is consistent, every solution can be viewed as one particular solution plus a solution from the associated homogeneous system $Ax=0$.

7207.title: Nonisothermal Flow
7207.heading: Nonisothermal Flow
7207.content:
Nonisothermal flow couples a fluid's pressure and velocity equations to its temperature equation. Fluid motion advects energy, while temperature can change density, viscosity, and therefore the motion itself.

The coupling matters in heated liquids, gases, breathing flow, pipes, and other systems where the temperature range is not negligible. Consistent reference temperature, pressure, and property definitions are required for [[Temperature-Dependent Fluid Properties|temperature-dependent behavior]].

7210.title: Nonbasic Variable
7210.heading: Nonbasic Variable
7210.content:
A nonbasic variable is set to zero in the current basic solution of a linear program. Its objective-row coefficient indicates whether allowing it to enter the basis can improve the objective.

A simplex pivot selects an entering nonbasic variable and a leaving [[Basic Variable]], then performs row operations to establish the new basis.

7225.title: Noetherian Ring
7225.heading: Noetherian Ring
7225.content:
A Noetherian ring is a ring in which every [[Ideal]] is finitely generated. Equivalently, every nonempty collection of ideals has a maximal member and every ascending chain of ideals eventually becomes stationary.

This finiteness condition supports decomposition and computation. Quotients of Noetherian rings remain Noetherian, and the [[Hilbert Basis Theorem]] extends the property from a ring to its polynomial rings.

7258.title: Nilradical
7258.heading: Nilradical
7258.content:
The nilradical is the [[Radical of an Ideal]] for the zero ideal. It consists exactly of the [[Nilpotent Element]]s of a ring and is the intersection of every [[Prime Ideal]].

Quotienting a ring by its nilradical yields a [[Reduced Ring]]. This operation removes nilpotent elements without changing the underlying set of prime ideals that determines the ring's spectrum.

7261.title: Nginx
7261.heading: Nginx
7261.content:
Nginx is a web server that can act as the public [[Reverse Proxy]] for a Linux-hosted ASP.NET Core application. It listens for HTTP or HTTPS traffic and passes application requests to a Kestrel service.

The Nginx configuration identifies the upstream address, certificate material, and forwarded request headers. Separating these responsibilities keeps Kestrel behind the public network boundary.

7264.title: Nilpotent Element
7264.heading: Nilpotent Element
7264.content:
A nilpotent element is a ring element r for which rⁿ = 0 for some positive integer n. Every nonzero nilpotent element is a [[Zero Divisor]].

All nilpotent elements together form the [[Nilradical]]. Passing to the quotient by that ideal removes nonzero nilpotents and produces a [[Reduced Ring]], retaining the ring's prime support while discarding nilpotent thickness.

The source derives the basic power laws of rings and uses repeated multiplication to distinguish elements whose positive powers become zero. Such elements exhibit how ring multiplication can behave differently from multiplication in a domain or field.

7273.heading: Newton's Second Law
7273.content: Newton's second law states that resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, $F=dp/dt$. For constant mass it reduces to $F=ma$, so acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force, proportional to that force, and inversely proportional to mass. The momentum form also applies when mass changes.

The method can converge rapidly near a simple root, but it requires derivatives and a suitable starting value. A zero or small derivative can make an iteration fail or jump away.

7285.content:
Newton divided-difference interpolation represents a polynomial incrementally using products $(x-x_0)\cdots(x-x_{k-1})$ and coefficients from [[Divided Difference|divided differences]].

Its main advantage over the Lagrange form is extensibility: adding one new data point adds one new term rather than forcing a complete recalculation.

7288.title: NewSQL
7288.heading: NewSQL
7288.content:
NewSQL describes database systems that seek distributed scalability while retaining relational interfaces and transactional guarantees associated with traditional SQL systems. They redesign execution, concurrency, and partitioning rather than simply placing an unchanged database on more machines.

The category is broad; a system's actual consistency, failure behavior, workload assumptions, and scaling limits matter more than the label.

7291.content:
A new-player playtest observes someone encountering the game without prior knowledge of its controls, rules, or goals. It reveals whether the opening experience supports discovery, forms an accurate mental model, and communicates enough information for independent action.

Because a person can be new only once, coaching destroys the evidence. The facilitator should note hesitation and interpretation before explaining what the design was supposed to mean.

7294.heading: Neutral Playtest Observation
7294.content:
Neutral playtest observation records what players do, say, attempt, and appear to misunderstand without coaching them toward the intended solution. The facilitator introduces the session, watches and listens, and reserves interpretation or discussion until it cannot alter the observed behavior.

Useful records distinguish direct events from inferences. "The player selected the door three times" is evidence; "the door is confusing" is a diagnosis to evaluate with the rest of the session.

7297.heading: Neutral CAD Exchange Format
7297.content:
A neutral CAD exchange format carries geometry through a published representation that multiple vendors can interpret. Formats such as STEP and IGES reduce dependence on a particular authoring application but may omit feature history, constraints, parameters, or product-specific semantics.

The receiving model should therefore be checked for changed units, missing faces, disconnected regions, and altered topology. Portability is achieved by exchanging a common subset, not by preserving every property of the native file.

7300.title: Neuron Activation
7300.heading: Neuron Activation
7300.content:
Neuron activation is the production of an output signal by a neuron. A biological neuron becomes more likely to fire as relevant input signals accumulate, while an [[Artificial Neuron]] calculates a numerical output from its weighted input and activation function.

Activation need not be a binary event in an artificial network. A [[Sigmoid Activation Function]] produces values between zero and one, a [[Tanh Activation Function]] ranges from negative one to one, and a rectifier passes positive values while suppressing negative ones.

7302.sourceSearchName: neuron activation space neuron activation space

7303.sourceSearchName: neuron activation space neuron activation space
7303.title: Neuron Activation Space
7303.heading: Neuron Activation Space
7303.content:
Kelleher distinguishes an activation space from the raw [[Model Input Space|input space]] and the [[Model Weight Space|parameter space]]. In his geometric example, weighted inputs are represented in the activation space where a threshold decision is applied. The resulting [[Decision Boundary]] can also be projected back to the original input coordinates.

The distinction is useful because an input case, the weights used to transform it, and the transformed value on which a unit acts are different objects. For a neuron, a weighted sum is followed by an [[Activation Function]] that maps it to the neuron's output activation. The activation-space view helps explain how a boundary produced after weighting corresponds to classifications of original inputs.

7306.sourceSearchName: neuromuscular junction on a chip neuromuscular junction on a chip
7306.title: Neuromuscular Junction-on-a-Chip
7306.heading: Neuromuscular Junction-on-a-Chip
7306.content:
A neuromuscular junction-on-a-chip cultures motor neurons and skeletal muscle in connected microenvironments. Neurites grow toward the muscle and form bioelectrical connections through which neural stimulation produces muscle contraction.

Using patient-derived neurons can model diseases whose origin lies in communication between tissue types rather than in muscle alone.

7309.title: Neuromorphic Computing
7309.heading: Neuromorphic Computing
7309.content:
Neuromorphic computing builds hardware around many interconnected, low-power [[Spiking Neuron|spiking units]] rather than using only a centrally sequenced processor. Signals are exchanged as events over time, and the units can communicate in parallel while maintaining local state.

Kelleher discusses this architecture as a possible way to reduce energy demands for some neural computations. Its computational organization is distinctive, but a chip's resemblance to biological neurons does not make it a complete model of a human brain or automatically replace ordinary deep-learning hardware. The book also notes the challenge of creating algorithms and software for such large parallel systems.

7311.sourceSearchName: neural network weight neural network weight
7311.title: Neural Network Weight
7311.heading: Document

7312.sourceSearchName: neural network weight neural network weight
7312.title: Neural Network Weight
7312.heading: Neural Network Weight
7312.content:
A neural-network weight is a numerical parameter applied to one input of an [[Artificial Neuron]]. Multiplying each input by its weight determines how strongly and in which direction that connection influences the neuron's [[Weighted Input]].

Training changes weights to reduce a [[Loss Function]]. A positive or negative value can make a connection excitatory or inhibitory in the simplified computational model, while the collection of learned weights stores much of the network's fitted behavior.

Kelleher interprets a neuron's input weights as a vector. For a threshold unit with two inputs, changing that vector rotates the [[Decision Boundary]] because the boundary is orthogonal to the weight direction. Weights can also be collected into a matrix for [[Layer Matrix Computation]], so all neurons' weighted sums in a fully connected layer are calculated together.

7313.sourceSearchName: neural network weight neural network weight
7313.title: Neural Network Weight
7313.heading: References

7314.sourceSearchName: neural network parameter update neural network parameter update
7314.title: Neural Network Parameter Update
7314.heading: Document

7315.sourceSearchName: neural network parameter update neural network parameter update
7315.title: Neural Network Parameter Update
7315.heading: Neural Network Parameter Update
7315.content:
A neural-network parameter update changes weights and biases so that future predictions produce a smaller [[Loss Function|loss]]. For each parameter, training calculates how the loss changes and moves the value a small amount in the opposite direction.

The [[Gradient]] gathers these local changes for all parameters. [[Backpropagation]] makes the required derivative information available from the output layer back through the earlier layers, and a [[Neural Network Optimizer]] controls how the updates are applied.

Kelleher distinguishes the gradient-calculation step from the update rule. For a connection weight, the error sensitivity computed at its destination neuron is combined with the activation received from its source neuron; [[Gradient Descent]] then changes that weight by a [[Learning Rate|learning-rate-scaled]] step in the loss-reducing direction. Backpropagation supplies the sensitivity, but it is not itself the only possible choice of weight-update rule.

7316.sourceSearchName: neural network parameter update neural network parameter update
7316.title: Neural Network Parameter Update
7316.heading: References

7317.sourceSearchName: neural network optimizer neural network optimizer
7317.title: Neural Network Optimizer
7317.heading: Document

7318.sourceSearchName: neural network optimizer neural network optimizer
7318.title: Neural Network Optimizer
7318.heading: Neural Network Optimizer
7318.content:
A neural-network optimizer is an algorithm that determines how weights and biases are changed to reduce the [[Loss Function]]. It converts derivative information into a sequence of [[Neural Network Parameter Update|parameter updates]].

Different optimizers can make training faster or more stable, enabling larger networks to be fitted efficiently. The optimizer does not define the network's architecture or loss; it governs the procedure used to move the adjustable parameters toward lower error.

7319.sourceSearchName: neural network optimizer neural network optimizer
7319.title: Neural Network Optimizer
7319.heading: References

7320.sourceSearchName: neural network layer neural network layer
7320.title: Neural Network Layer
7320.heading: Document

7321.sourceSearchName: neural network layer neural network layer
7321.title: Neural Network Layer
7321.heading: Neural Network Layer
7321.content:
A neural-network layer is a group of computational units occupying the same stage of an [[Artificial Neural Network]]. An input layer receives the observations, successive layers transform those values, and an output layer produces the network's final result.

A [[Hidden Layer]] lies between the external input and output. Layers may be [[Dense Layer|densely connected]] so every neuron feeds every unit in the following layer, or use specialized patterns suited to a particular task.

Kelleher notes that input-layer locations simply present stored values; they do not perform the learned weighted processing of later layers. In a dense network, all the neurons of the next layer can calculate their weighted sums together through [[Layer Matrix Computation|one vector–matrix operation]]. Counting only layers with learned weight matrices explains [[Neural Depth Counting|network depth]].

7323.sourceSearchName: neural network explainability gap neural network explainability gap
7323.title: Neural Network Explainability Gap
7323.heading: Document

7324.sourceSearchName: neural network explainability gap neural network explainability gap
7324.title: Neural Network Explainability Gap
7324.heading: Neural Network Explainability Gap
7324.content:
The neural network explainability gap arises because a trained network’s conclusion is distributed across many learned weights rather than a human-readable sequence of rules. Inspecting the computations may not yield a meaningful reason for the output.

The gap is especially important in medicine, safety, and governance, where users need grounds for trust and appeal. Evaluation must therefore include behavior on new inputs, uncertainty, monitoring, and complementary explanation methods.

Kelleher identifies three obstacles to interpreting a deep model: its scale, distributed internal representations, and successive transformations of inputs as they pass through layers. [[Neural Feature Visualization]] investigates what might trigger internal units, while a [[Neural Attribution Map]] estimates contributions to particular outputs. These views make the model more inspectable, but neither turns distributed computation into a complete human-readable reason for a decision.

7325.sourceSearchName: neural network explainability gap neural network explainability gap
7325.title: Neural Network Explainability Gap
7325.heading: References

7327.sourceSearchName: neural network classification neural network classification
7327.title: Neural Network Classification
7327.heading: Neural Network Classification
7327.content:
Neural network classification learns a mapping from input attributes to output class representations through weighted connections and nonlinear activation functions. Training adjusts the weights from differences between predicted and target outputs.

Multilayer networks can form nonlinear decision boundaries that a single perceptron cannot. Performance should be checked on observations not used to update the weights.

7330.sourceSearchName: neural network bias neural network bias
7330.title: Neural Network Bias
7330.heading: Neural Network Bias
7330.content:
A neural-network bias is a numerical parameter added to an artificial neuron's weighted input before applying its [[Activation Function]]. It shifts the neuron's propensity to activate independently of the current input values.

The opposite of a bias can be interpreted as a threshold that the weighted sum must cross. Like a [[Neural Network Weight]], the bias is adjusted during training to reduce prediction loss.

In Kelleher's geometric example, changing the weight direction rotates a neuron's [[Decision Boundary]], while changing the bias translates that boundary away from the origin. A constant input fixed at one can treat the bias as another learned weight, allowing the same weighted-sum and matrix calculations to include it without a separate special-case update.

7333.sourceSearchName: neural model composition neural model composition
7333.title: Neural Model Composition
7333.heading: Neural Model Composition
7333.content:
Model composition feeds the output of one learned mapping into another mapping. Kelleher first illustrates this by passing a weighted credit score into a decision rule; the combined process answers a more complex question than either component alone.

An [[Artificial Neural Network]] repeats this principle: each neuron computes a comparatively simple function, and successive layers use earlier activations as their inputs. The network's overall input-to-output function emerges from those connected transformations. Nonlinear [[Activation Function|activation functions]] are crucial because composing weighted sums without nonlinear steps would still produce only a linear mapping.

7335.heading: Document

7336.sourceSearchName: neural feature visualization neural feature visualization
7336.title: Neural Feature Visualization
7336.heading: Neural Feature Visualization
7336.content:
Feature visualization seeks inputs that strongly trigger a selected behavior inside a neural network, such as a hidden unit's activation. Kelleher describes starting with a generated input and iteratively changing it until the chosen response increases, then viewing the result to investigate what the unit may detect.

The method can make learned representations more inspectable than raw weights alone. However, the constructed input is evidence about the model's response, not necessarily a typical real-world example or a full explanation of the model's final decision. It complements [[Neural Attribution Map|attribution]] and other views of the [[Neural Network Explainability Gap]].

7339.sourceSearchName: neural feature learning neural feature learning
7339.title: Neural Feature Learning
7339.heading: Neural Feature Learning
7339.content:
Neural feature learning uses a network's internal transformations to construct useful representations from input data instead of requiring every derived feature to be hand-designed. Kelleher contrasts a manually calculated feature, such as a ratio derived from raw measurements, with the representations a deep model can learn from many high-dimensional examples.

A hidden unit may respond to a learned combination of earlier features, and later units can compose these partial results. This is why [[Deep Neural Network|deep networks]] can work with complex image or language inputs, but it does not remove the need for thoughtful data selection or evaluation. The learned features are useful to the task, not automatically transparent to a human observer.

7341.sourceSearchName: neural depth counting neural depth counting
7341.title: Neural Depth Counting
7341.heading: Document

7342.sourceSearchName: neural depth counting neural depth counting
7342.title: Neural Depth Counting
7342.heading: Neural Depth Counting
7342.content:
The depth of a feedforward [[Deep Neural Network|neural network]] counts learned layers rather than merely every visible row of its diagram. The input layer presents values but has no preceding weight matrix of its own; hidden layers and the output layer perform learned transformations. Kelleher therefore counts depth as hidden layers plus the output layer, or equivalently the number of weight matrices traversed.

This convention clarifies why a diagram with one input layer, three hidden layers, and one output layer has depth four. It also makes a [[Time-Unrolled Recurrent Network|time-unrolled recurrent network]] appear deep across a long sequence even though its recurrent weights are reused at every time step.

7343.sourceSearchName: neural depth counting neural depth counting
7343.title: Neural Depth Counting
7343.heading: References

7344.sourceSearchName: neural credit assignment problem neural credit assignment problem
7344.title: Neural Credit Assignment Problem
7344.heading: Document

7345.sourceSearchName: neural credit assignment problem neural credit assignment problem
7345.title: Neural Credit Assignment Problem
7345.heading: Neural Credit Assignment Problem
7345.content:
In a multilayer network, the training data specify an expected final output, not the correct activation for each hidden neuron. Credit assignment asks how much each hidden unit and weight contributed to the network's output error so that parameter changes can be directed appropriately.

[[Backpropagation]] addresses the problem by calculating local error gradients at the output and propagating them backward through the connections. A [[Gradient Descent|weight-update method]] can then use the resulting derivatives. Kelleher distinguishes these steps: assigning sensitivity to internal parameters is necessary before choosing how to change those parameters.

7346.title: Neural Credit Assignment Problem
7346.heading: References

7347.sourceSearchName: neural attribution map neural attribution map
7347.title: Neural Attribution Map
7347.heading: Document

7348.sourceSearchName: neural attribution map neural attribution map
7348.title: Neural Attribution Map
7348.heading: Neural Attribution Map
7348.content:
An attribution map displays which inputs or internal activations a neural network relies on for a particular output. Kelleher describes saliency or heat-map views that estimate how strongly the output relates to neurons in earlier layers.

This helps inspect a decision pathway in a large network whose representations are distributed across many units. The map is a model-analysis aid, not an exact human-readable chain of reasoning or proof that the model used only the highlighted information. Alongside [[Neural Feature Visualization]], it addresses part of the [[Neural Network Explainability Gap]] by making internal contributions easier to examine.

7351.heading: NetworkStream
7351.content:
`.NET`'s `NetworkStream` exposes data moving through a connected socket through the standard `Stream` interface. Code can read and write bytes without implementing packet reassembly itself because the transport and socket layers supply the ordered stream abstraction.

The stream still represents a remote and potentially slow source. Reads may block or complete with partial data, and disposal, timeouts, encoding, and higher-level message framing must be managed deliberately.

7354.content:
Network-based misinformation detection uses who transmits information to whom and the resulting graph structure. Abnormal patterns, such as sending similar material to many strangers, can reveal suspicious behavior even when individual messages appear ordinary.

Graph constraints can also preserve similarity between connected users in a reduced feature space. Care is required because malicious accounts may deliberately follow regular users to disguise their structure.

7357.title: Network Socket
7357.heading: Network Socket
7357.content:
A network socket is the software endpoint used to communicate through a network port. Its specification includes the address family, socket type, and protocol needed to create a compatible connection or datagram endpoint.

Client code connects a socket to a remote endpoint, while server code binds and listens for incoming connections. The socket exposes low-level control but leaves application message framing and error handling to the program.

7360.title: Network Topology
7360.heading: Network Topology
7360.content:
A network topology describes the arrangement of nodes and communication links. Physical topology records the actual infrastructure, while logical topology describes the path and direction by which nodes exchange data.

Topology affects routing, cost, resilience, and failure concentration. Software should account for those effects without assuming that the logical path visible to an application exactly matches the underlying cables or radio links.

The network security layer controls and observes communication among systems. [[Firewall]] rules restrict traffic at boundaries, while an [[Intrusion Detection System]], [[Intrusion Prevention System]], and [[Security Event Monitoring]] help identify or stop suspicious behavior.

This layer is strongest when controls are distributed rather than concentrated at one perimeter. Internal segmentation and monitoring can constrain movement after an attacker or malicious program reaches the network.

7366.content:
A network port is a numeric transport-layer endpoint that directs incoming traffic on a host to the intended application or service. An IP address identifies the host interface, while the port distinguishes processes or logical services on that host.

Servers bind a [[Game Network Socket]] to an address and port so clients know where to send traffic. Firewalls and address translation may need explicit rules for the selected transport and port range.

Game traffic should avoid unnecessary payload because bandwidth, serialization time, and packet frequency all contribute to network cost. A receiver must validate packet type, length, ordering information, and claimed values before applying them to game state.

The freedom reduces control over event order, so stories and dependencies must tolerate multiple sequences or use selected gates. Choke points should be deliberate because they concentrate movement and conflict.

7390.sourceSearchName: net present value net present value
7390.title: Net Present Value
7390.heading: Net Present Value
7390.content:
Net present value sums future cash inflows and outflows after discounting them to a common present time. A positive value indicates that expected discounted benefits exceed costs under the chosen rate.

For interdependent subprojects, changing the running order changes the dates of costs and benefits and can therefore change the portfolio's value.

NPV can compare a stream of recurring cloud-service payments with the up-front cost of owned infrastructure by expressing both at the same present time. It can also convert a capital amount into an equivalent recurring stream. A positive NPV indicates that discounted benefits exceed the initial and continuing costs under the chosen discount rate.

For an energy-technology investment, the same calculation places equipment cost, future fuel savings, operation and maintenance, and eventual residual value on one present-value basis. Different payment timing can change which technical alternative is economically preferable. [[Internal Rate of Return]] is the discount rate at which this NPV becomes zero, so it gives a related test against the cost of capital.

7393.content: Net cost savings are the present value of conventional-energy costs avoided by a new system minus its added investment and operating costs, adjusted for residual value. 7396.title: Nested Transaction
7396.heading: Nested Transaction
7396.content:
A nested transaction decomposes a parent transaction into inner transactions with their own execution boundaries. The structure expresses internal parallelism, partial recovery, or modular composition while preserving rules about the parent's final outcome.

Nesting semantics determine when an inner result becomes visible and whether its effects are undone if the parent later aborts.

7399.heading: Nested Model Comparison
7399.content:
A nested model comparison evaluates two models when the smaller model's terms are all contained in the larger one. The change in likelihood and degrees of freedom can be assessed to determine whether the added parameters materially improve fit.

This comparison can guide choices such as entering a continuous predictor directly or as several category indicators. A better-fitting complex model must still justify the additional parameters and yield a scientifically interpretable representation.

For least-squares models, the source compares the reduction in residual sum of squares with the additional degrees of freedom. Analysis of variance uses this relationship to test whether a block such as several interaction terms improves the model beyond sampling variation.

7402.content:
A neighborhood-level graph feature summarizes the local subgraph surrounding a node. Degree, neighbor attributes, local density, and small motif counts are common examples.

Local features are relatively inexpensive and often interpretable. They may fail to distinguish nodes whose immediate neighborhoods look alike but whose positions in the full network differ.

7405.title: Neighborhood Component Analysis
7405.heading: Neighborhood Component Analysis
7405.content:
Neighborhood component analysis learns a projection by maximizing the expected leave-one-out performance of stochastic nearest-neighbor classification. Each observation chooses another case as a neighbor with probability that decreases with projected squared distance.

The probability of correct classification is the total selection probability assigned to same-class neighbors. Optimizing this objective favors a local geometry in which each case is surrounded by useful label peers.

7408.title: Negative Transfer
7408.heading: Negative Transfer
7408.content:
Negative transfer occurs when imported source knowledge makes target performance worse than learning from target evidence alone. It can arise from mismatched feature distributions, label meanings, class boundaries, or source quality.

Detecting negative transfer requires a target-grounded baseline and validation that separates genuine help from added sample size. Selective weighting, source rejection, or weaker coupling can limit damage from an unsuitable domain.

7411.content:
A negative input edge occurs when a digital control was pressed in the previous frame and is released in the current frame. It identifies the end of one held interval.

Release-sensitive actions can charge while held and resolve on this edge, or stop a mode exactly when control ends. Like the [[Positive Input Edge]], it depends on retaining both current and previous states.

7414.heading: Negative Feedback in Game Balance
7414.content:
Negative feedback in game balance makes success increase later resistance or makes failure reduce it. It narrows differences among players or keeps challenge near a target level.

Moderate negative feedback can sustain uncertainty and recovery. If it is too strong, leading becomes a disadvantage and outcomes swing artificially, weakening the connection between decisions and results.

7417.title: Negative Cycle
7417.heading: Negative Cycle
7417.content:
A negative cycle is a [[Graph Cycle]] whose edge weights sum to a negative value. Repeating the cycle reduces a route's accumulated cost every time it is traversed.

If such a cycle is reachable in a shortest-path problem, no finite shortest path exists for affected destinations because the path length can always be made smaller. This is more than a limitation of [[Dijkstra's Algorithm]]; the requested optimum itself is undefined.

7420.title: Negative Exponent
7420.heading: Negative Exponent
7420.content:
A negative exponent denotes the [[Reciprocal]] of the corresponding positive power. For nonzero (a),

$$a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^n}.$$

This interpretation follows from (1=a^0=a^{n-n}=a^na^{-n}). It also means that taking a reciprocal reverses the sign of an exponent: (1/a^{-n}=a^n). Negative exponents do not make the value itself negative; for example, (2^{-3}=1/8). They describe position between numerator and denominator rather than arithmetic sign.

7423.title: Nearest-Neighbor Texture Filtering
7423.heading: Nearest-Neighbor Texture Filtering
7423.content:
Nearest-neighbor texture filtering chooses the texel center closest to a requested texture coordinate and returns that texel's value. It is inexpensive and preserves hard pixel boundaries.

When a texture is magnified, the method produces visible blocks; when minified, it can flicker or alias because many source texels compete for one pixel. The look can be intentional for pixel art but unsuitable for smoothly detailed surfaces.
